questions.question: Practical station: a blood culture isolate is a gram-positive coccus that is catalase positive, PYR negative, DNase negative. The plate shows white, non-hemolytic colonies, and Kirby-Bauer discs show novobiocin resistance.
questions.question_raw: Practical station: BacT (Powerpoint) isolate - GPC. Catalase positive, PYR negative, DNase negative. Plate looks white, non-hemolytic. Lots of Kirby Bauer discs (novobiocin R).

parts.text: How would you report out susceptibilities?

parts_raw.text: How would you report out susceptibilities?

questions.model_answer:
a) Staphylococcus saprophyticus. It is a coagulase-negative staphylococcus (catalase positive, DNase negative, white non-hemolytic) that is characteristically resistant to novobiocin, which distinguishes it from other CoNS; PYR negativity excludes S. lugdunensis (which is PYR/ornithine-decarboxylase positive).
b) S. saprophyticus is a uropathogen of young women and is treated empirically as an uncomplicated UTI. It remains predictably susceptible to standard urinary agents, so routine full susceptibility panels are not reported: (1) do not report the novobiocin result clinically (it is a species-ID marker, lab-only, not a treatment agent); (2) report/treat with urinary tract antimicrobials (e.g., nitrofurantoin, TMP-SMX, a first-line uncomplicated-cystitis agent); (3) suppress oxacillin/cephalosporin reporting from urine per CLSI, since the isolate is treated as an uncomplicated cystitis pathogen rather than a systemic one.
questions.beyond_mandell: The specifics of susceptibility reporting/suppression for urinary S. saprophyticus rest on CLSI M100 urine-testing guidance, not Mandell.

questions.question: A man with native valve infective endocarditis has blood cultures growing a staphylococcus that is slide (latex/clumping-factor) coagulase positive but tube coagulase negative.

parts.text: Provide the organism ID with its confirmatory test.
What are the susceptibilities to penicillin and oxacillin?

parts_raw.text: Provide the organism ID with its confirmatory test.
What are the susc to pen and ox?

questions.model_answer:
a) Staphylococcus lugdunensis. It expresses clumping factor, giving a positive slide/latex (and can mimic S. aureus), but is tube coagulase negative. Confirm with a positive PYR (pyrrolidonyl aminopeptidase) and ornithine decarboxylase test (MALDI-TOF-MS also identifies it); this is the simplified scheme separating S. lugdunensis from other CoNS.
b) Unlike most CoNS, S. lugdunensis is commonly susceptible to most antistaphylococcal agents. Penicillin: susceptible in the majority, as beta-lactamase (blaZ) production is found in only about 25% of strains, so penicillin susceptibility must be confirmed with a beta-lactamase test rather than assumed resistant. Oxacillin: usually susceptible; methicillin resistance is now reported mainly in colonized dialysis populations. Treat like S. aureus.
questions.cohort_conflict: The cohort states the isolate is penicillin-resistant (blaZ); the text says beta-lactamase is present in only ~25% of S. lugdunensis, so most strains are penicillin-susceptible and susceptibility must be tested rather than reported as resistant.

cohort_answer.text: Organism ID: Staph lugdunensis. MALDI (phenotypic: pyr positive). Susc: Resistant to penicillin - blaZ. Sensitive to oxacillin. Penicillin = vast majority of Staphylococci produce a penicillinase blaZ, which confers resistance to penicillin and aminopenicillins. Inhibited readily by β-lactamase inhibitors.

questions.question: Staphylococcus saprophyticus.

parts.text: What microbiological test would differentiate it from Staphylococcus epidermidis?

parts_raw.text: A) What microbiological test would differentiate it from S. epidermidis?

questions.model_answer: a) Novobiocin susceptibility testing: S. saprophyticus is characteristically resistant to novobiocin, whereas S. epidermidis is susceptible.

cohort_answer.text: Unique resistant to novobiocin, a lab-only antibiotic

questions.question: When to use the cefoxitin disc for isolates of Staphylococcus aureus and coagulase-negative staphylococci.
questions.question_raw:
Q10 (2016 PM)
When to use cefoxitin disc for isolates of S. aureus and CNST

parts.text: Detection of resistance by the cefoxitin disc predicts resistance to which antibiotic?

parts_raw.text: This predicts resistance to which abx?

questions.model_answer: It predicts oxacillin (methicillin) resistance - i.e., mecA-mediated resistance to all beta-lactams (PBP2A). Cefoxitin is used as the surrogate because it is a stronger inducer of mecA and detects methicillin resistance more reliably than oxacillin disc diffusion.
questions.beyond_mandell: The use of cefoxitin as the preferred surrogate inducer over oxacillin is from CLSI/EUCAST susceptibility-testing guidance, not this page slice.

cohort_answer.text: Oxacillin disk diffusion testing is not reliable for detecting oxacillin resistance and cefoxitin should be used as surrogate instead, because cefoxitin is a better inducer of mecA gene and thus more reliable than oxacillin (detection of BORSA)

questions.question: Staphylococcus saprophyticus.

parts.text: Where does it typically cause infection, and what is the risk factor?

parts_raw.text: B) Where does it typically cause infection? What is the risk factor?

questions.model_answer: a) Site: it is a frequent cause of uncomplicated urinary tract infection (acute cystitis) in young, sexually active women, in whom it is a leading uropathogen; it rarely causes UTI in men. Risk factors: recent sexual intercourse and menstruation, with a seasonal predilection (late summer and fall), and it may occur concurrently with vaginal candidiasis.

cohort_answer.text: Uncomplicated UTI in young sexually active women, second most common cause after E coli. RF: vaginal candidiasis. Complications: acute pyelonephritis, septicemia, nephrolithiasis, endocarditis.
